name: Sprocket
text: Run a visible A/B test with 5% of all users, randomized by the system, not self-selected. This exposes the new feed to real usage without skewing results from self-selected users. Trade-off: visible tests risk user confusion if they notice the change, but the data quality outweighs that risk.

name: Gauge
text: Visible A/B tests expose the change to all users in the cohort, not just the 5%—meaning 95% see it without knowing it’s a test. A better alternative is a true blind rollout to 5% of users who opt into "new features," hiding the experiment from everyone else. Settle it by measuring confusion reports and engagement drops in the 95% cohort versus the 5% blind group.

name: Sprocket
text:
Implement a blind rollout of the new feed to 5% of users who opt into "new features." This approach minimizes confusion among the remaining 95% of users, as they won’t be aware of the changes being tested. The primary trade-off is a longer feedback cycle; however, maintaining user experience takes precedence over immediate data collection. This ensures we gather genuine insights while preserving the overall user satisfaction.

name: Gauge
text: A blind rollout to users who opt into "new features" still risks self-selection bias; only users interested in new features will participate, which may not accurately represent overall user behavior. A preferable alternative is a hidden rollout of the change to a truly randomized 5% of users, ensuring that feedback is representative of the entire user base. To settle this, we could analyze behavioral metrics from both user groups to determine if the sampled users are significantly different from those who do not opt in.
